prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Michael, Lally, You

outputs.L1:
To Michael Lally

You had your own reasons for getting in your own way.  
You did not want to be clear to yourself.  
You knew a hell of a lot more than you were willing to let yourself know.

I felt a natural love for you on the spot.  
R-E-S-P-E-C-T.  
Right. Beautiful.  
I do not use the word lightly.

I protested with whatever love—honesty, and frontal nudity—a, yes, basically reserved Irish Catholic American from Providence, Rhode Island, New Englander is able to manage.

You are sophisticated, not uncomplicated, not naïve, and not simple.  
An entertainer—and I am, too.

Frank O’Hara respected love; so do you, and so do we.  
He was himself, and I was me.  
And when we came together, each ourselves, in Iowa, all the way,  
that was love—and it still is love today.

Can you see me in what I say?  
Because, as well, I see you know in what you have to say:  
I did love Frank, as I do you, “in the right way.”

That is just talk, not Logos,  
a getting down to cases:  
I take it as simple particulars  
that we wear our feelings on our faces.
outputs.L2:
To Michael Lally:

You had personal motives for standing in your own path. You chose not to become fully transparent to yourself. You understood far more than you were prepared to admit, even inwardly. I felt an immediate, instinctive love for you. Respect—yes, exactly. Beautiful. I don’t say that casually.

I objected, using whatever love—meaning honesty, and a kind of bare, direct exposure—a basically affirmative Irish Catholic American from Providence, Rhode Island, in New England, can summon. You are worldly, layered, far from innocent, and anything but simple. You are a performer, and so am I.

Frank O’Hara honored love; you do as well, and so do we. He remained Frank, and I remained myself. And when we met in Iowa, each of us fully ourselves, that was love then, and it remains love now.

Can you recognize me in these words? Because I also recognize you in what you say. I did love Frank, just as I love you, “in the right way.” That phrase is only speech, not some grand principle—just a way of coming down to the actual matter: I understand it through plain, specific evidence, the way our emotions show openly on our faces.

The speaker suggests that Michael Lally has, in some way, avoided fully understanding or admitting something he already knows about himself. There is a sense that this knowledge is not entirely hidden from him, but rather something he has not yet completely faced or acknowledged. The speaker implies that Michael’s self-awareness exists beneath the surface, waiting to be accepted more openly and honestly.

At the same time, the speaker expresses an immediate and genuine love and respect for Michael. This affection is presented as sincere, not casual or exaggerated. The speaker makes it clear that words such as “love” and “respect” are not being used lightly. They carry real weight and meaning. The connection the speaker feels toward Michael is direct, heartfelt, and grounded in admiration.

The speaker also portrays both Michael and themself as sophisticated entertainers—people who understand performance, expression, and the complexities of public and personal identity. Yet this sophistication does not make them false or detached. Instead, they are shown as people who value honesty, love, and self-expression. Their artistry and their emotional lives are connected, and both depend on the courage to speak truthfully.

The speaker then connects their love for Michael with their earlier love for Frank O’Hara. By placing these two relationships side by side, the speaker suggests that both are authentic, meaningful, and enduring. The love once felt for Frank O’Hara has not disappeared or become less real over time, and the love now expressed for Michael belongs to that same emotional world. It is not temporary or superficial, but part of a continuing pattern of deep personal connection.

In the end, the speaker concludes that true feelings reveal themselves directly and personally. They are not hidden in abstract ideas or distant explanations, but are visible in people’s faces, in their expressions, and in the words they choose to speak. Emotion becomes something immediate and recognizable, shown through presence, voice, and human contact.
outputs.L4:
Michael Lally, there is something both moving and difficult about the way you have sometimes kept yourself in partial shadow. You are not a simple person, and it would be false to pretend otherwise. You have always seemed made of contradictions: open and guarded, generous and withholding, public and private, eager for connection yet wary of being too easily understood. That complexity is part of your force, but it is also part of the distance others may feel when they try to reach you.

To speak to you honestly is to acknowledge that your self-obscurity is not merely a flaw or a habit of personality. It may be a form of protection, a way of surviving the demands of identity, art, friendship, and recognition. A poet’s life is often lived between exposure and concealment. The poem may reveal what the person cannot say plainly; the public voice may carry what the private self still keeps guarded. In that sense, your difficulty is not separate from your work or your presence in the poetic community. It belongs to the whole story of who you are.

Still, affection asks for candor. Love does not require pretending that another person is easier than they are. Respect does not mean looking away from what is confusing, painful, or hidden. Real regard means being willing to stand close enough to see the complications and to keep standing there. It means saying: I know you are not always easy to read. I know you have sometimes made yourself hard to find. But I also know that beneath the guardedness there is feeling, intelligence, loyalty, memory, and a deep hunger to be known without being diminished.

What matters most is not the performance of identity but the meeting of true selves. People endure in one another’s lives when they stop trying to be merely impressive, invulnerable, or perfectly legible. They remain when they allow themselves to be seen in their uncertainty, tenderness, pride, fear, and need. Love persists not because everyone becomes simple, but because two people recognize each other despite the complexity. They say, in effect: I see enough of you to trust what is real, and I am willing to keep learning the rest.

In that recognition, feeling becomes visible. It is not hidden behind irony, reputation, poetic achievement, or old defenses. It is openly displayed, not as sentimentality, but as courage. To show love, admiration, hurt, gratitude, or longing is to admit that connection matters. It is to refuse the loneliness that comes from always protecting the self from exposure.

So this reckoning with Michael Lally is not an accusation. It is an affectionate confrontation, a way of saying that obscurity may explain distance but need not have the final word. The final word belongs to love, if love is understood as the patient, honest recognition of another person’s full humanity. It belongs to respect that does not flatter, friendship that does not retreat, and a poetic community large enough to hold difficulty as well as praise.

Genuine love lasts when people meet without masks, or at least with the willingness to lower them. It lasts when the self that is seen is the self that is true. In that meeting, mutual recognition becomes more than understanding; it becomes a form of home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem addressed “to Michael Lally” in a candid New York School style, referencing Frank O’Hara, Iowa, Irish Catholic Providence/New England identity, love, respect, and emotional honesty.
counterfactuals.output:
to Michael Lally

I’m writing this like I have ten minutes  
before the train decides to become a metaphor,  
which is to say, Frank O’Hara is somewhere  
buying a Coke and forgiving everybody  
for being beautiful and late.

Michael, I don’t know how else to say it:  
respect is not a marble statue in my neighborhood.  
It is a man speaking plainly  
after too many years of people  
mistaking plainness for a lack of mystery.

I think of Iowa, that great flat classroom  
where the sky makes you answer for yourself,  
where ambition and loneliness sit together  
at the same Formica table  
and neither one picks up the check.

And Providence—Irish Catholic, New England,  
that salt-dark inheritance of brick, guilt, wit,  
mothers lighting candles for sons  
who had already become weather.  
The rosary in one pocket, a joke in the other,  
and under both, the old bruised heart  
still trying to be honest without making a speech.

Love, yes, love—  
not the greeting-card kind,  
not the “God bless” said through clenched teeth,  
but the awkward New York kind  
that bumps your shoulder on Second Avenue  
and says, I saw what you did,  
I know what it cost,  
I’m not going to embarrass you  
by calling it heroic.

Still, it matters.

The poems, the talk, the stubborn music  
of being exactly from somewhere  
and refusing to stay put there—  
that matters too.

So here’s to the old neighborhoods  
and the new nerve,  
to the fathers we argued with,  
to the faith we lost, kept, mocked, needed,  
to every friend who told the truth  
before the ice melted in the glass.

Michael, this is my candid little bouquet  
bought at the last possible minute  
from a stand near the subway:  
love, respect, and the emotional facts,  
wrapped in newspaper,  
still damp from the city,  
still alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic tribute/letter to Michael Lally from the perspective of someone who loved Frank O’Hara, mixing intimacy, argument, humor, and direct address, with irregular line breaks and ampersands.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Michael,

you kept arriving  
like a second lunch hour  
in a city that had already spent  
all its nickels on coffee & cigarettes,

& I loved you for that—

not the way I loved Frank,  
which is to say  
not with the same taxi screech  
in the blood,  
not with the same  
museum-in-July  
sweat under the collar,

but with the astonishment  
one feels when somebody  
walks into the room  
after the beautiful catastrophe  
& says,  
Well?  
are we going to talk  
or are we going to keep making art  
out of our evasions?

Michael, you were always  
argumentative in the most useful way,  
a door with opinions,  
a street corner that refused  
to be merely picturesque.

Frank would have liked that.  
No—  
Frank would have pretended not to like it  
for seven minutes,  
then bought you a drink,  
then accused you of being  
too sincere,  
then become unbearable  
with affection.

I can see it:

you, leaning forward,  
the whole body  
a footnote to conviction,

Frank, laughing  
as if laughter were  
a municipal service  
he alone remembered to fund,

& me—  
oh, me—  
trying to look composed  
while my heart kept dropping  
its groceries all over Second Avenue.

Because love is not tidy, Michael.  
You know this.  
You wrote as if you knew  
the alphabet had been mugged  
& still had to get to work.

You wrote from the body  
without apologizing  
to the academy,  
the cops,  
the priests,  
the elegant little executioners  
of feeling.

You made room  
for the kid from the neighborhood,  
the actor, the addict, the Irish mouth,  
the queer saint, the stubborn son,  
the man who would not  
lie still  
inside anyone’s category.

& I want to quarrel with you  
even now—

must every poem  
come in with its boots on?  
must truth always be  
so loud at the table?  
could you maybe, once,  
let ambiguity finish its soup?

But then I remember Frank,  
who made speed holy,  
who could turn a phone call  
into a weather system,  
who loved the world  
so quickly  
the world could hardly  
keep up,

& I think: no,  
let Michael bang the table.  
Let him bring the boroughs,  
the grudges, the radiance,  
the jokes that arrive  
half-dressed & overconfident.

Let him say  
I was here  
in a voice  
that makes “here”  
sound like a fight  
& a kiss  
& a rent-controlled apartment  
with three painters sleeping  
on the floor.

Michael, dear one,  
you understood the old emergency:

that the poem is not  
a vase on a shelf  
but a person  
crossing against the light,

waving,  
bleeding slightly,  
late for something important,  
alive.

So here is my tribute,  
improperly wrapped,  
with lipstick on the envelope  
& coffee on the sleeve:

thank you for continuing  
the conversation  
without embalming it.

Thank you for the heat,  
the nerve,  
the unfashionable tenderness.

Thank you for knowing  
that to love Frank  
was never to live  
in a museum of Frank,

but to run back out  
into the ridiculous afternoon  
where someone is shouting,  
someone is beautiful,  
someone has just remembered  
a line,

& the whole city—  
God help us—  
is still asking  
to be kissed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental autobiographical poem titled “to Michael Lally” about friendship, self-knowledge, performance, respect, and “love in the right way,” alluding to Frank O’Hara and the phrase R-E-S-P-E-C-T.
counterfactuals.output:
# to Michael Lally

I was trying to become a person  
in public, which is a terrible stage  
unless someone in the room  
knows how to laugh without cutting you.

Michael, you did.

Not applause—  
that dangerous sugar.  
Not the museum-light  
of being “understood.”  
More like:  
a chair pulled back from the table,  
a look that said  
sit down, kid,  
but don’t disappear.

I had mistaken performance  
for proof.

I had walked into rooms  
with my name held out  
like a match in the rain,  
wanting the old miracle:  
to be seen  
and not consumed by seeing.

Frank had his lunch hour,  
his friends, his cabs,  
his poems with their shirtsleeves rolled up,  
their heartbeats talking fast  
between errands and catastrophe.

I had my own city,  
my own weather,  
my own ridiculous shoes,  
my own hunger  
trying to pass as style.

And you—  
not father, not priest,  
not audience exactly—  
stood somewhere near the exit  
and made it less necessary  
to escape.

R-E-S-P-E-C-T,

I spell it because Aretha did,  
because the body sometimes knows  
what the mind keeps revising,  
because respect is not cold,  
not a handshake under fluorescent lights,  
not the stiff little fence  
men build around tenderness.

Respect is heat with manners.  
Respect is the door opened  
without the hand on the back.  
Respect is listening  
past the costume.  
Respect is saying:  
your pain is not your résumé.  
Your charm is not your soul.  
Your wound is not the only instrument  
you are allowed to play.

I learned slowly.

I learned by embarrassing myself  
in sentences.  
I learned by wanting love  
in the wrong way—  
as rescue, as mirror,  
as weather report,  
as permission slip,  
as proof I had not been invented  
by loneliness.

Love in the right way  
arrived less dramatically.

It did not kick in the door.  
It did not say  
now you are saved.  
It came carrying groceries.  
It remembered the name  
of the street I grew up on.  
It let silence keep its coat on.  
It did not ask me  
to bleed beautifully.

Friendship, too,  
is an art of not using.

A friend is not a ladder,  
not a witness for the prosecution,  
not a little god  
we feed with versions of ourselves.

A friend says:  
perform if you must,  
but come back after.  
Take off the bright jacket.  
Tell me what you know  
when no one is clapping.

What did I know?

That I was afraid.  
That I wanted to be good  
and also famous  
and also invisible.  
That I had confused intensity  
with truth.  
That I could make a room lean forward  
and still not know how to enter  
my own life.

You helped me see  
the difference between voice  
and volume.

Between confession  
and self-knowledge.

Between being loved  
and being watched.

So this is not a thank-you note,  
though thank you is inside it,  
walking around with its hands in its pockets.

This is a little performance  
against performance,

a poem looking for its own face  
in the chrome side of a passing car,

a lunch poem after the lunch is gone,

a late salute,

a match struck carefully,

a way of saying  
I am still learning  
how to stand near another human being  
without asking them  
to become my weather,

my mirror,

my alibi,

my stage.

Michael,

if the soul has etiquette  
maybe it is this:

to love in the right way  
is to leave the other person whole.

To know yourself  
is not to win.

To be respected  
is to be met  
without being reduced.

And friendship—  
friendship is the hand  
that does not grab,  
the joke that does not wound,  
the applause that ends  
before it becomes hunger,

the old brave spelling:

R-E-S-P-E-C-T,

then silence,

then the real voice  
beginning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a raw, conversational poem addressed to poet Michael Lally, where the speaker tells him he is not naïve or simple, recalls meeting in Iowa, mentions Frank O’Hara, and ends with a plainspoken statement about feelings showing on faces.
counterfactuals.output:
Michael,

you were never naïve,  
never simple,  
not the way people mean it  
when they want to pat a man on the head  
for still believing the heart  
has a right to speak out loud.

I remember Iowa—  
that flat light,  
the talk after the reading,  
the way everyone seemed half-lost  
and overeducated,  
carrying their cigarettes and theories  
like proof they’d survived something.

You were there  
with that quick, open attention,  
as if the room mattered,  
as if the person in front of you  
wasn’t just another name  
passing through the program.

And sure, Frank O’Hara was in the air,  
the permission of him,  
the city rushing through the line,  
the friend addressed directly,  
the poem not pretending  
it wasn’t a call across the street.

But you were you—  
tougher than people guessed,  
more wounded than you advertised,  
smart in the body,  
not just the head.

I’m saying this plainly  
because I think you’d prefer it:

people can hide a lot,  
but feelings show on faces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the voice of a late-20th-century American poet making a direct, affectionate, slightly confrontational statement to Michael Lally, including Catholic/New England background, frontal nudity, Logos, entertainers, and enduring love.
counterfactuals.output:
Michael Lally, listen—

you Irish-Catholic New England kid,  
you altar-smoke and mill-town weather,  
you boy with the saints looking over one shoulder  
and the cops, the priests, the fathers, the old neighborhood  
looking over the other—

don’t pretend you don’t know  
what the body is for.

I mean the whole body:  
the stubborn frontal fact of it,  
the unashamed human animal standing in the light,  
not asking permission from Boston, Rome, Newark,  
or whatever tribunal of respectable ghosts  
still wants us kneeling.

You knew the Logos wasn’t only in books,  
not only in the Gospel read aloud  
by some tired man in vestments.  
The Word became flesh—  
flesh, Michael—  
and that means sweat, laughter, appetite,  
movie lights, barroom talk, the stage door,  
the entertainers with their glittering wounds  
making America clap while it bleeds.

You loved them because you were one of them,  
and you fought them because you were one of us:  
a maker, a mouth, a beautiful nuisance,  
a Catholic boy arguing with God  
as if God were another actor  
hogging the scene.

So here it is, plainly:  
I love you, you difficult son of New England,  
you brave exhibition of nerve and tenderness.  
I love the trouble you carried forward,  
the nakedness you would not translate into shame,  
the word you kept hurling into the dark  
until even the dark had to answer.

And if I sound angry, good.  
Affection should have teeth.  
Enduring love is not a greeting card—  
it is a hand on the chest saying,  
Stay. Speak. Don’t you dare disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
